Transformers: Attention for Words, DNA and Proteins

Step 1: attention by hand · Step 2: word order · Step 3: a tiny transformer on DNA · Step 4: tokens beyond words · Step 5: scale
The recurrent network of Part 3 reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward. Information from far back has to survive many steps, and the steps cannot run in parallel. A transformer looks at the whole sequence at once: every element (a token) can directly look at every other token, however far apart, and decide how relevant it is. This mechanism is called attention. It is the core of large language models, and also of protein models such as ESM and AlphaFold.

Step 1: Attention by hand

Every word asks every other word: how relevant are you to me? All of attention is one expression: ||[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right) V||]
Each word ||(i||) (a token) gets three short lists of numbers (vectors) of length ||(d||) (here ||(d = 4||)):
  • a query ||(\mathbf{q}_i||): what am I looking for?
  • a key ||(\mathbf{k}_i||): what am I?
  • a value ||(\mathbf{v}_i||): what do I pass on if someone looks at me?
Stacking them, one row per word, gives the matrices ||(Q||), ||(K||) and ||(V||). The computation has three steps: 1. Score of word ||(i||) looking at word ||(j||): multiply matching numbers, add up, divide by ||(\sqrt{d}||) to keep the scores in a good range: ||[s_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j}{\sqrt{d}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \sum_{m=1}^{d} q_{im}\, k_{jm}||]2. Weights: the softmax turns each row of scores into positive weights that add up to 1 (100%). The temperature ||(T||) of the slider divides the scores first (||(T = 1||) is the standard transformer; smaller ||(T||) sharpens, larger ||(T||) spreads): ||[a_{ij} = \frac{e^{s_{ij}/T}}{\sum_{l} e^{s_{il}/T}}, \qquad \sum_j a_{ij} = 1||]3. Output of word ||(i||): the weighted mix of all the values: ||[\mathbf{o}_i = \sum_{j} a_{ij}\, \mathbf{v}_j||]In a real transformer, the vectors come from the word embeddings ||(X||) multiplied by learned matrices: ||(Q = X W_Q||), ||(K = X W_K||), ||(V = X W_V||). Here we write them by hand with four readable features (living thing, place, pronoun, describing word), so you can check the result. In a real model, "it" also learns about "tired" or "wide" in an earlier layer; here we give "it" that hint directly in its query.
With ||(n = 11||) words and ||(d = 4||) numbers per word: ||[Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{11 \times 4} \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d}} \in \mathbb{R}^{11 \times 11} \;\longrightarrow\; A = \text{softmax}(\cdot) \in \mathbb{R}^{11 \times 11} \;\longrightarrow\; A V \in \mathbb{R}^{11 \times 4}||]The score matrix has one row per word that looks and one column per word looked at. The output is again one vector of 4 numbers per word, now mixed with its context. With several heads, each head ||(h||) has its own ||(W_Q^{(h)}, W_K^{(h)}, W_V^{(h)}||) and computes this in parallel.

Step 2: Word order

Attention alone does not know where each word is: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same.
The scores depend only on the words' numbers, not on their positions. If we shuffle the words, every word still finds the same partners with the same weights; only the rows and columns of the attention map are shuffled. So the summary of the sentence (the average of all outputs, which is what our DNA classifier in Step 3 uses) is exactly the same for "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". The fix is positional encoding: before attention, we add to each word's numbers a pattern that depends only on its position (below). Now the same word at a different position has different numbers, and the order matters. Remember the RNN notebook: we gave the hour of the day as sine and cosine, like a clock hand, so that 23:00 and 00:00 are close. Positional encoding uses the same trick with several clock hands turning at different speeds, so that every position gets its own pattern and nearby positions have similar patterns.

The top rows change quickly from one position to the next, the bottom rows slowly, so no two columns are the same. <strong>Right:</strong> three of those rows drawn as curves: sine waves of different speeds, like the hands of a clock. Together they tell the model where each token is.</span></span></div>

Step 3: A tiny transformer on DNA

Does motif A come before motif B? A question about order and distance, which a CNN cannot answer.
In bacterial promoters (the switch in front of a gene), the -35 box (TTGACA, motif A) comes before the -10 box (TATAAT, motif B). Every sequence here contains both boxes once, 10 to 24 letters apart, at random positions. In half of the sequences they are in promoter order (A before B, label 1); in the other half the order is reversed (label 0). Which motifs are present gives no clue: only their order does. In the DNA motif Colab notebook (Part 2), a 1D CNN found a motif with a filter and global max pooling, which keeps the best score of each filter and forgets where it was found. Here that is exactly the problem: the CNN can see both motifs but not which comes first, so it should stay near chance (50%). The transformer compares every position with every other position, and with positional encoding it knows where each token is. Tokens: the transformer reads the DNA as overlapping 6-letter words (6-mers), as the DNABERT model does: positions 1-6, 2-7, 3-8, and so on. Each motif then appears as one token.

The data, generated here at random with a fixed seed: 3,000 training, 500 validation and 1,000 test sequences, each 64 letters long (half in each class). The models learn only from the training sequences; the test sequences are used once, to measure accuracy. Two examples from the test set:

Layer Output shape (tokens × numbers) Parameters
Input: DNA letters 64 0
6-mer tokens (overlapping) 59 0
Embedding (4,096 possible tokens → 32 numbers) 59 × 32 131,072
+ positional encoding (sine/cosine, fixed) 59 × 32 0
Self-attention (2 heads) + add & normalize 59 × 32 4,288
Feed-forward (two Linear layers, ReLU) + add & normalize 59 × 32 4,256
Average over tokens 32 0
Linear (classifier) 2 66
Total: 139,682 parameters, almost all of them in the embedding table (32 numbers for each of the 4,096 possible 6-mers).Estimated training time: about 7 s

Train Model trains the transformer and the CNN live; Load Pre-trained loads both trained longer beforehand (shown when the notebook opens).
Each 6-mer token is turned into 32 numbers (the embedding), and the positional encoding is added. One self-attention layer with 2 heads lets every token look at every other token; a small feed-forward network then processes each token on its own. "Add & normalize" means the layer's input is added back to its output (a shortcut that makes training easier) and rescaled. Finally the tokens are averaged into one summary of the sequence, and a linear layer decides between "A before B" and "B before A". This is one transformer encoder layer; large models stack dozens of them. The CNN is the one from the DNA motif notebook: 4 filters 8 letters long, global max pooling and a linear layer. Load Pre-trained loads both models trained for 40 epochs, with or without positional encoding, following the switch above.

Test accuracy, pre-trained models (40 epochs) (1,000 sequences never seen in training)

Chance (guessing) 50%
1D CNN (Part 2) 53.4%
Transformer 100.0%

Look inside: the attention map

Which tokens does the transformer look at? The orange and blue lines mark the two motif tokens.
Each row is one token that "looks", each column a token being looked at; darker means more attention. Every token is a 6-letter piece of the sequence, so there are 64 - 6 + 1 = 59 tokens. The dashed orange lines cross at the motif A token and the dashed blue lines at the motif B token. A dark column means many tokens look at that position: if it sits on a colored vertical line, the whole sequence is looking at that motif. The plot on the right shows only the two motif rows. The network was never told where the motifs are, yet it learns to focus on them. In the models we trained, the two heads split the work: one looks almost only at motif A, the other at motif B (which head takes which motif changes from one training run to the next). Each token's output then carries the numbers of both motifs, including their positional encodings, so the last layers can compare the two positions. Heads in large models are usually much harder to interpret than this.

Test sequence 1: truly B before A; the transformer says B before A (100% confident). On average, head 1 puts 99% of each token's attention on motif A and 0% on motif B.Left: gray squares are attention weights (black = high). The dashed orange lines mark the motif A token and the dashed blue lines the motif B token: the vertical line is the column (the motif being looked at), the horizontal line is the row (the motif token doing the looking). Right: the black curves are the two motif rows; the shaded bands show where the motifs are.

Step 4: Tokens beyond words

A token can be a word, a DNA 6-mer, a patch of an image, or an amino acid in a protein.
A Vision Transformer cuts an image into small square patches and treats them as a sequence of tokens, each with a positional encoding that says where the patch was. Attention then lets every patch look at every other patch, so a spot on one side of the leaf can be related to a spot on the other side from the very first layer. A CNN (Part 2) only sees small neighborhoods at first and needs many layers to cover the whole leaf.

Proteins: what does a protein language model look at?

ESM-2 is a published protein language model from Meta AI (Lin et al., Science, 2023), trained on about 65 million protein sequences, one amino acid per token. Without ever seeing a structure, some of its attention heads follow which amino acids touch in the folded protein. Here: ubiquitin (76 amino acids).
ESM-2 ("Evolutionary Scale Modeling") was built by the protein team of Meta's Fundamental AI Research lab and published by Lin et al. (2023) in Science. The goal was to test whether a language model trained only on protein sequences learns enough biology to predict a protein's 3D structure. The same paper introduced ESMFold, which predicts full 3D structures from ESM-2's internal representations, and the ESM Metagenomic Atlas with more than 617 million predicted structures of proteins from environmental samples.
  • Training data: protein sequences from UniRef (UniProt Reference Clusters, September 2021 release), a public database of known protein sequences grouped by similarity. Training samples evenly across about 43 million clusters (UniRef50), drawing from about 138 million sequences (UniRef90), so the model sees about 65 million different sequences.
  • Training task: 15% of the amino acids of each sequence are hidden (masked) and the model predicts them from the rest. No structures and no labels are used.
  • Sizes: from 8 million parameters (6 layers) to 15 billion parameters (48 layers). The weights are freely available, which is why we can run them here and in Colab.
  • Contact maps: following Rao et al. (2021), a simple logistic regression combines the attention maps of all heads into the contact prediction shown below.
Remember the autoencoder's encoder? ESM-2 is a transformer encoder trained much like the denoising autoencoder: some amino acids in each sequence are hidden, and the model must fill them in from the rest. No labels and no structures were used, only sequences. To fill in a hidden amino acid well, it helps to know which other amino acids touch it in the folded protein, so some attention heads end up following the 3D contacts. Unlike our autoencoder, ESM-2 keeps one embedding per amino acid instead of one small bottleneck. This is the idea of pre-training: train once on huge data, then reuse or adapt the model for many tasks (structure, function, effects of mutations). DNABERT (Ji et al., 2021) does the same for DNA, pre-trained on the human genome with 6-mer tokens like ours, and Vision Transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) do it for images. Session 3 shows how to use such pre-trained models in code. The maps were computed beforehand for three sizes of ESM-2 and are loaded from the workshop repository. True contacts: pairs of amino acids closer than 8 Å in the crystal structure (PDB 1UBQ). The attention map shown is averaged in both directions (i looks at j, and j looks at i). ESMFold turns ESM-2's representations into 3D coordinates. AlphaFold 2 (Jumper et al., 2021) reaches the same goal differently: its attention layers read an alignment of many related sequences together with the protein. Try the hands-on Colab notebook to run ESM-2 on your own protein and explore every layer and head.

Step 5: Scale

The same building block, stacked and scaled up.
Model Parameters What it does
Our DNA transformer (Step 3) 140 thousand one layer, A before B
ESM-2 small (Step 4) 7.5 million proteins, 6 layers
ESM-2 medium 34 million proteins, 12 layers
ESM-2 large 148 million proteins, 30 layers
GPT-2 small (2019) 124 million text, 12 layers
ESM-2 largest 15 billion proteins, 48 layers
GPT-3 (2020) 175 billion text, 96 layers
Today's largest language models hundreds of billions or more text, images, code (many sizes are not published)
The core operation does not change: attention, feed-forward, add & normalize, repeated layer after layer. What grows is the number of layers, the length of the embeddings, the number of heads, and above all the amount of training data and computing power. Step 4 showed one effect: the same protein model, made larger, predicts contacts much better. To see a full language model (GPT-2) running in your browser, try the Transformer Explainer: poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer.

data.text/markdown:
What to notice

  • Attention lets every token score every other token (query · key), turn the scores into weights (softmax), and take a weighted mix of their values, all in parallel.
  • Attention alone is order-blind; positional encoding tells the model where each token is. With it, a one-layer transformer relates two motifs far apart, which a CNN with pooling cannot.
  • Tokens can be words, DNA k-mers, image patches or amino acids. Models pre-trained on huge data, such as ESM-2, learn useful structure (like protein contacts) without being told.

Questions for discussion

  1. What would a token be in your own data (field images, sensor readings, sequences)?
  2. Why can a transformer relate two distant motifs more easily than the RNN from Part 3?
